summary: LUNARCHIVE is an interactive web platform that tells the stories of the machines NASA left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. We developed it as a website with a built-in 3D game, in English and Arabic. It addresses the challenge by giving each abandoned machine its own voice: each relic introduces itself in the first person, with real NASA facts, live photos, maps and a quiz. Children can drive and fly in 3D to rebuild each machine part by part, and live its real mission from launch to its real ending. This matters because children mostly hear about the machines still working, while the explorers that finished their work, and taught us how to land and explore, are forgotten. LUNARCHIVE makes sure they are not.
details:
LUNARCHIVE is a web platform that gives voices to the machines NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. It has three parts.
What it does and how it works. The Relic Vault holds 28 relics. Each one has a first-person voice that children can hear read aloud, a real story, the science it made, a fun fact, the reason it was left behind, a quiz, and live NASA photos. The Surface Landing Map shows real NASA maps of the Moon and Mars, with each relic at its landing coordinates. The Relic Rescue Rover is a 3D game with three worlds. Children drive across the Moon and Mars, or fly a ship through deep space, find glowing beacons, and rebuild each relic by choosing the part that does the job. Be the Relic lets a child become one machine and live its real mission in order, from launch to the ending that really happened. Correct quiz answers earn badges, and the badges feed a printable certificate.
Benefits and intended impact. The project makes real space history understandable and memorable for children aged 8 to 14. It gives teachers a ready 20-minute lesson. It keeps families safe: there is no account and no personal data is collected. It is free, runs in any web browser, and works in English and Arabic, with keyboard and touch controls. The intended impact is that children learn to care about the explorers that finished their work, and understand why those machines still matter.
Tools and technologies. HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no build step. Three.js for the 3D game and starfield. Tailwind CSS for layout and Font Awesome for icons. Google Fonts for typography. The Web Speech API for read-aloud. Live NASA photos from the NASA Image and Video Library, and NASA Solar System Treks maps. The site is hosted on Vercel and the code is public on GitHub. We used a PowerPoint presentation for the pitch.
Creativity. Each machine speaks in the first person, so a child hears the story from the machine itself. The game lets children choose how to rebuild, and the mission simulator follows each machine’s real timeline, including the ending, which is never changed. Original cartoon characters and an animated astronaut that floats through the site were drawn for the project.
What the team considered. We considered accuracy, so every story is built from NASA’s own pages and data. We considered safety and privacy, so children need no account and nothing about them is collected. We considered accessibility, so the site works in two languages, with both keyboard and touch, and offers read-aloud for children who are still learning to read. We considered sustainability, so the site is free and runs in a browser with no installation.
